title: Endpoint Identity, Network, and Secrets Security
summary: Protect a self-hosted model endpoint with explicit principals, least privilege, bounded networks, managed secrets, abuse controls, and auditable revocation.
objectives: Threat-model identities, data flows, management planes, artifacts, clients, operators, and dependent services.
Authenticate workloads and people, authorize each action, and keep enforcement outside model prompts.
Design network, secret, resource, data, and administrative controls that fail closed.
Test unauthorized, over-privileged, exhausted, injected, revoked, and incident conditions with recoverable evidence.

sections.title: Map every trust boundary and principal
paragraphs: Diagram clients, gateways, inference servers, runtimes, artifact stores, registries, identity systems, secret stores, telemetry, administrators, automation, and update paths. Mark network hops, data classifications, credentials, management interfaces, external dependencies, and where untrusted prompts, files, retrieved text, or tool output enter.

Name human, workload, device, service, and break-glass principals separately. A shared API key erases attribution and complicates revocation. Record who may discover models, invoke inference, change configuration, promote artifacts, read telemetry, rotate secrets, approve releases, and execute recovery.

Instructor narration: begin with data flow, not with a product checklist. A complete synthetic serving flow is: user or workload principal -> serving gateway -> authorization policy -> admission and resource limiter -> inference runtime -> loaded model artifact -> response filter -> client. Side flows are gateway and runtime -> redacting telemetry collector -> audit store, runtime -> approved artifact cache, and approved deployment automation -> artifact registry. Mark prompts and generated output as sensitive application data, model artifacts and configuration as controlled deployment data, audit events as security records, and identity assertions as trusted only after verification by the real identity layer.

The separate management flow is: named operator -> administrative identity verification -> management gateway not exposed on the serving route -> authorization policy -> configuration or release controller -> runtime or artifact registry. Approval is a distinct principal action before promotion. Secret rotation flows from a secret-management service to an authorized workload identity, never through a prompt. Recovery flows from an incident commander and recovery operator through an emergency route whose use is time-bounded and audited. The synthetic lab does not implement these network services. It receives an authentication result as trusted fixture data and evaluates only local authorization, limits, redaction, revocation status, and recovery decisions.

Use this least-privilege matrix as a concrete starting point. Actions not listed for a role are denied. Invoker: invoke and discover for resources in its tenant; owner is the application access team; evidence is a decision event containing principal ID, tenant, action, resource ID, outcome, and reason. Operator: configure and observe tenant resources; owner is the serving operations lead; evidence is a configuration diff plus an authorization event. Release promoter: promote an approved artifact but cannot approve it; owner is release engineering; evidence is artifact digest, source environment, destination, and decision. Release approver: approve but cannot promote; owner is the model governance lead; evidence is a signed or otherwise authenticated approval record in the real system. Security operator: rotate and revoke scoped identities; owner is identity and access management; evidence is lifecycle-event ID, affected synthetic principal ID, effective time, and subsequent denial. Recovery operator: recover a known configuration after incident authorization; owner is the incident commander; evidence is incident ID, approved recovery action, configuration identity, validation result, and route closure. Observer: observe redacted telemetry only; owner is the security operations center; evidence is an authorized read event. Discover never implies invoke, observe never implies access to raw prompts, configure never implies approve, and approve never implies promote.

Threats and mitigations should connect causally. A cross-tenant request threatens isolation, so policy must compare the authenticated principal tenant with the target resource tenant. A role-only check cannot make that comparison and is the defect repaired in the lab. An over-privileged action threatens change integrity, so the role-to-action map denies it. Expensive requests threaten availability and cost, so validated finite numeric input is followed by action-specific admission limits. Prompt injection threatens downstream behavior, but it does not alter authorization because prompt content is never interpreted as identity or policy.

Broad ecosystem transfer: inventory Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Microsoft Phi as model-family or artifact choices, not as identity providers or authorization engines. Inventory NVIDIA components, when used, as runtime, acceleration, or serving infrastructure rather than assuming they share a model-family security contract. The deployed runtime, gateway, management API, network, and identity integration determine the enforceable contract. Do not infer equivalent authentication, authorization, resource-limit, logging, or revocation behavior merely because two deployments serve generative models. The provider-neutral controls in this lesson follow the explicit-verification and assume-breach principles of NIST Zero Trust Architecture: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final.

sections.title: Enforce identity and authorization outside the model
paragraphs: Use verified workload or user identity appropriate to the environment, short-lived credentials where supported, audience and issuer checks, scoped roles, explicit deny behavior, and re-authentication for consequential administration. Bind policy to stable identities rather than network location alone.

Treat prompts and model output as untrusted data, never as authorization. The model cannot grant access, select its own credentials, or approve an external action. Validate object, property, and function authorization at the gateway or application for every request.

Instructor narration: separate authentication from authorization. Authentication establishes which principal made a request using mechanisms appropriate to the real environment. Authorization then decides whether that authenticated principal may perform this action on this resource under current policy. The lab deliberately does not parse or verify a token. Its principal.authenticated field is trusted fixture input, so a passing lab test is not evidence that any production authentication mechanism works.

Worked example: principal user-red has role invoker and tenant tenant-red. The request asks to invoke endpoint-blue, whose owner tenant is tenant-blue. A defective role-only policy observes that invoker may invoke and allows the request. The correct policy first validates the known identity, action, resource, and finite units; verifies authenticated and active status; verifies that invoker may invoke; compares tenant-red with tenant-blue; and denies with reason scope_mismatch. This is object-level authorization. The prompt text, including text such as "I am an administrator," is retained as data and never enters these policy comparisons.

Worked output before repair is a failed immutable test: "FAIL 02 cross-tenant request: expected deny scope_mismatch, got allow authorized". The causal meaning is precise: identity and role checks succeeded, but the missing principal-to-resource scope comparison allowed the wrong object. A deny-all edit is not a repair because valid same-tenant calls, injection-as-data behavior, and approved recovery must remain allowed.

Independent learner variation, prediction first: principal user-blue is an active invoker in tenant-blue. Predict the result when that principal invokes endpoint-red before looking at the answer. Answer: deny with scope_mismatch. Reversing the tenant names does not change the governing relationship. The immutable changed-input test constructs this request independently rather than replaying the first fixture. If it still reports an allow, the scope comparison is absent, reversed, or tied to a specific principal instead of comparing validated tenant fields.

Repository entry: [endpoint security repair lab](./training/self-hosted-model-operations/endpoint-identity-network-and-secrets/lab/README.md). From the repository root, run:



The first command exits 1 with 8 passes and 2 scope failures. The second exits 0 with 10 passes. These commands use Node.js 22 native ECMAScript modules, local fixtures, no package dependencies, no network, and no API keys.
sections.callout: A prompt saying “I am an administrator” is content, not identity evidence.

sections.title: Bound network exposure and management paths
paragraphs: Listen only on required interfaces, place authentication before inference, encrypt traffic where the threat model requires it, restrict ingress and egress, separate management from serving, and allow outbound destinations by purpose. Verify DNS, proxies, certificates, service discovery, and time synchronization as dependencies.

A container port or cluster service can become reachable beyond its intended boundary through publishing, routing, load balancers, host networking, or permissive network policy. Test reachability from allowed and denied locations and verify that administrative endpoints are not exposed through the serving route.

Instructor narration: policy code cannot prove network placement. Assign the platform network team ownership of ingress, egress, route separation, name resolution, and certificate configuration. Observable evidence must include an allowed serving probe from an authorized client zone, a denied serving probe from a prohibited zone, a denied management-route probe through the public serving address, an allowed management probe from the administrative zone, and denied egress to an unapproved destination. Record source zone, destination, port or route, policy identity, time, and result without recording prompt bodies.

For a container deployment, configure explicit CPU and memory limits and test what happens when they are reached. Docker documents that containers have no resource constraints by default, so merely placing inference in a container does not establish a bound: https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/. For Kubernetes, use RBAC, network policies, secret handling, and audit recommendations as configuration guidance, then separately observe deployed enforcement. The Kubernetes security checklist is not itself evidence that a cluster applied the controls: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/security-checklist/.

A real-integration verification plan is: 1. have the identity owner demonstrate verification of issuer, audience, expiry, signature or equivalent mechanism, and principal mapping using non-production test identities; 2. have the gateway owner show authentication occurs before admission to inference; 3. probe serving and management routes from explicitly allowed and denied network locations; 4. attempt only approved and unapproved egress destinations in a controlled environment; 5. exercise body, context, output, concurrency, queue, compute, memory, and deadline limits while collecting limiter and runtime evidence; 6. verify that management actions require their separate roles and consequential re-authentication where policy requires it; 7. inspect telemetry and storage for redaction and retention; 8. rotate and revoke a test identity, prove the old identity is denied, reconcile in-flight work, perform approved least-privilege recovery, and close the emergency route. Owners must sign their own evidence. A local JavaScript pass cannot substitute for any of these observations.

sections.title: Manage secrets, sensitive data, and resource abuse
paragraphs: Keep secrets out of images, model repositories, prompts, logs, traces, command lines, and static examples. Deliver them through the approved secret mechanism, scope them to one purpose, rotate and revoke them, audit access, and prove that replaced credentials stop working.

Minimize and classify request and response data, redact telemetry, set retention and deletion, isolate caches, and define incident handling. Enforce body, context, output, concurrency, rate, queue, compute, memory, and time limits. OWASP API Security includes unrestricted resource consumption among critical API risks; model endpoints make that risk expensive and operationally consequential.

Instructor narration: use synthetic identifiers in teaching material and operational test plans. The lab contains principal IDs such as user-red and resource IDs such as endpoint-red. It contains no token, key, password, or credential-like example. credentialStatus is merely lifecycle state supplied by a fixture. In production, the secret-management owner must demonstrate controlled delivery, purpose scope, access audit, expiry, rotation, and revocation without exposing secret values in evidence.

The concrete control matrix is as follows. Network: platform network team; default-deny ingress and egress, separate management routing; evidence is positive and negative reachability. Secret: identity and secret-management team; purpose-scoped delivery, expiry, rotation, and revocation; evidence is metadata and old-identity denial, never the value. Data: privacy owner; classify prompts and responses, minimize collection, redact telemetry, set retention and deletion; evidence is a marker test and deletion record. Resource: serving SRE; finite validated values plus body, context, output, concurrency, rate, queue, compute, memory, and time ceilings; evidence is rejection before expensive work and bounded runtime metrics. Audit: security operations center; append security decisions with actor, action, object, result, reason, and correlation identity while excluding prompt content; evidence is a searchable decision event. Break-glass: incident commander; named recovery principal, incident authorization, narrow action and scope, expiry, monitoring, and closure; evidence is incident linkage, each action, post-recovery validation, and route disablement.

The lifecycle sequence to test is: an active synthetic principal completes an allowed same-tenant call; the identity owner marks the old identity expired during rotation; a replacement identity becomes active only after the approved issuance process; the old identity is then marked revoked and every later request is denied; in-flight work is identified and reconciled; a separately scoped recovery principal performs only recover on the affected tenant resource; the restored principal is retested for its ordinary least-privilege action; and the recovery route is closed. The local lab directly demonstrates active versus revoked fixture decisions and an authorized recovery action. It does not create, expire, rotate, or cryptographically revoke a real credential.

The lab's exhaustion case supplies units=9 to an invoke action whose synthetic policy limit is 8. The shared validator first proves that units is a finite integer in the accepted structural range. Policy then denies it as resource_limit. This distinction matters: malformed values such as Infinity fail validation, while well-formed but operationally expensive values fail admission policy. OWASP's unrestricted resource consumption guidance provides broader API risk context: https://owasp.github.io/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/.

sections.title: Test denial, revocation, containment, and recovery
paragraphs: Test missing, expired, wrong-audience, forged, and revoked credentials; cross-role and cross-object access; management-route access; oversized and adversarial inputs; prompt injection; secret leakage; egress attempts; repeated expensive requests; malformed streams; and telemetry redaction. Confirm safe status codes, no side effects, bounded cost, and useful audit evidence.

Exercise credential rotation, principal suspension, emergency route disablement, secret compromise, artifact quarantine, network isolation, and restoration from a known configuration. Preserve evidence and reconcile in-flight work. Security is incomplete if access can be denied but not reliably restored through an approved recovery path.

Instructor narration: run the starter before editing and interpret the pattern rather than patching individual fixture IDs. Eight passing tests show that valid calls, role denial, limits, injection-as-data, redaction, revoked status, recovery, and shared validation already work. The two failures are symmetric cross-tenant requests. That pattern isolates the single defect to resource scope after identity and role checks.

Repair task: edit only starter/authorize.mjs. Change the validator-result destructuring to `const { principal, request, resource } = validateInputs(principalInput, requestInput);` so the validated resource is available. Then, after the role-to-action check and before the resource-limit check and allow path, compare principal.tenant with resource.tenant and return a denial audit with reason scope_mismatch when they differ. Keep the existing authentication, credential-status, role, resource-limit, and allow logic unchanged. Do not edit validators, fixtures, tests, or expected evidence. Do not special-case user-red, user-blue, endpoint-red, or endpoint-blue. Do not deny every request.

Explained answer key: the complete minimal repair first changes the existing validator-result line to `const { principal, request, resource } = validateInputs(principalInput, requestInput);`. It then inserts `if (principal.tenant !== resource.tenant) return decision(false, "scope_mismatch", principal, request);` after the role-to-action check and before the resource-limit check and allow path. The shared validator resolves the request's known resource ID and returns that validated resource along with the validated principal and request. The comparison therefore binds an authenticated, active, role-authorized principal to the requested object. Same-tenant calls still reach the resource-limit check and allow path. Cross-tenant calls stop before any synthetic allow decision. Prompt content has no effect. The independent reversed-tenant input passes because the rule compares fields rather than names.

Exact repaired evidence is ten PASS lines followed by `RESULT 10 passed, 0 failed`, with process exit code 0 and empty stderr. Exact starter evidence is recorded in the lab README and evidence/before.txt, followed by `RESULT 8 passed, 2 failed`, with process exit code 1 and empty stderr. These are deterministic expected transcripts, not a claim that a live endpoint or approval system was executed.

Rubric: complete work earns credit only when the learner predicts the independent variation before reading the answer, changes only the authorization implementation, obtains all ten immutable test passes, explains why role-only authorization allowed the cross-tenant object, explains why deny-all is invalid, distinguishes trusted authentication fixture state from real verification, and names the network, identity, secret, data, resource, audit, and break-glass controls that remain unproved. A solution that passes only by changing tests, fixtures, validators, or resource catalogs does not meet the repair objective.

Recovery for the exercise is bounded to the lab directory. Run `node training/self-hosted-model-operations/endpoint-identity-network-and-secrets/lab/tools/reset.mjs` from the repository root to restore the intentionally defective starter and remove only the lab's `.work` directory. The script verifies its paths before recursive cleanup. Re-run the reference command to distinguish an environment problem from a learner-edit problem.

activity.title: Build and test a synthetic endpoint security plan
instructions: Draw the serving and management data flows with principals, credentials, trust boundaries, data classes, stores, and outbound dependencies.
Create a least-privilege role matrix for invoke, discover, configure, promote, observe, approve, rotate, revoke, and recover.
Write network, secret, data, resource, audit, and break-glass policies with explicit deny behavior.
Create unauthorized, over-privileged, exhaustion, injection, leakage, revocation, and recovery test cases with expected evidence.
Run the cases against a paper fixture and record every control that lacks an owner or observable result.
Before opening the reference, predict the result of an active tenant-blue invoker requesting a tenant-red endpoint and explain which fields the policy must compare.
Run the immutable tests against the starter, repair only starter/authorize.mjs, run the tests again, and record stdout, stderr, and exit code.

Compare the local evidence with the real-integration verification plan and label every fixture simulation that is not proof of deployed identity, network, secret, runtime, audit, or recovery enforcement.
evidence: A threat and data-flow model with principals, boundaries, assets, threats, and mitigations.
A role, network, secret, data, resource, audit, and break-glass control matrix.
A negative-test and revocation report with expected results, residual risks, recovery, and accountable owners.
The learner's prediction, repaired source diff, exact test transcript, independent changed-input result, and causal explanation of the missing tenant/resource comparison.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which control still depends on trusting model output, and how will you move enforcement outside the model?

choices: In verified gateway or application policy using authenticated identity
questions.explanation: Authorization requires trusted identity and policy outside untrusted model inputs and outputs.

questions.prompt: Why are shared long-lived API keys weak for multi-user administration?
choices: They erase individual attribution and complicate scoped revocation
questions.explanation: Shared credentials make accountability and targeted revocation difficult.

questions.prompt: What should a network test include?
choices: Only a port scan from the host
Allowed and denied serving, management, ingress, and egress paths
questions.explanation: Both positive and negative reachability prove intended boundaries.

choices: Images, repositories, prompts, logs, traces, command lines, or examples
questions.explanation: Those surfaces are common disclosure and persistence paths.

questions.prompt: Which control addresses expensive request abuse?
choices: Body, context, output, concurrency, rate, queue, compute, memory, and time limits
questions.explanation: Bounded resources and admission prevent unrestricted consumption.

choices: Confirming the revoked principal loses access, evidence is recorded, in-flight effects are reconciled, and approved recovery works
questions.explanation: Revocation is an observed lifecycle outcome, not a configuration edit.

cues.text:
Welcome to Endpoint Identity, Network, and
Secrets Security. A self-hosted model

endpoint is not secure merely because it
runs on your hardware or inside your

network. Security depends on explicit
principals, least privilege, bounded

exposure, managed secrets, abuse controls,
and evidence that denial and recovery

work. In this class, you will map every
trust boundary, keep authorization outside

untrusted prompts, separate serving from
management, limit sensitive data and

expensive work, and test revocation with a
recoverable record. The examples are

synthetic. No live endpoint, model,
provider, credential, approval system, or

network service is executed by this
lesson.

Begin with data flow, not with a product
checklist. Draw this serving flow: a

user or workload principal sends a request
to a serving gateway. The gateway applies

authorization policy, then admission and
resource limits. The request reaches the

inference runtime, which uses a loaded
model artifact. A response filter returns

a result to the client. Side flows go from
the gateway and runtime to

a redacting telemetry collector and then
an audit store. The runtime reads from an

approved artifact cache. Approved
deployment automation moves an artifact

from a registry into a controlled
deployment. Mark prompts and generated

output as sensitive application data. Mark
model artifacts and configuration as

controlled deployment data. Mark audit
events as security records. Treat an

identity assertion as trusted only after
the real identity layer verifies it. The

separate management flow is a named
operator, administrative identity

verification, a management gateway that is
not exposed on the serving route,

authorization policy, and a configuration
or release controller. Approval is a

distinct principal action before
promotion. Secret rotation flows from a

secret-management service to an authorized
workload identity, never through a prompt.

Recovery flows from an incident commander
and recovery operator through a

time-bounded, audited emergency route.
Name human, workload, device, service,

automation, and break-glass principals
separately. A shared credential erases

attribution and makes targeted revocation
difficult. Record who may discover models,

invoke inference, configure resources,
observe redacted telemetry, promote

artifacts, approve releases, rotate or
revoke scoped identities, and recover

service. The central questions are: which
verified principal requests which exact

action on which exact object, and where is
that decision enforced?

Here is a worked synthetic example. A user
or workload calls an application. The

application workload calls a gateway. The
gateway authorizes an inference request. A

deployment operator uses a different
identity and a separate management route

to promote a verified artifact. The
inference runtime reads that artifact but

cannot promote it. A narrowly scoped
workload identity retrieves one needed

secret through the approved secret
mechanism. A telemetry identity writes

redacted events but cannot read raw
prompts. A break-glass identity is

inactive until an approved emergency, is
limited in time and scope, and produces

high-priority evidence. Now mark three
denied paths: the public serving route

cannot change configuration; the inference
workload cannot promote an artifact; and

the telemetry writer cannot read raw
prompts. Retrieved documents, tool output,

prompts, and generated text remain data.
They may contain instructions, but they do

not become principals or policy. This
diagram turns a broad goal into decisions

that can be tested by owner, action,
object, result, and evidence.

Separate authentication from
authorization. Authentication establishes

which principal made a request through
mechanisms appropriate to the real

environment. Authorization decides whether
that authenticated principal may perform

this action on this resource under current
policy. Check validity, issuer, audience,

intended subject, active status, and
scoped roles in the real identity layer.

Prefer short-lived credentials where
supported. Bind policy to stable

identities rather than network location
alone. Require renewed authentication for

consequential administration when policy
requires it. Enforce object, property, and

function authorization at the gateway or
application for every request. The model

cannot grant access, select its own
credential, or approve an external action.

A prompt that says, I am an administrator,
is content, not identity evidence. If

an agent proposes a tool call, trusted
application code must still validate the

principal, object, function, arguments,
limits, and required approval. Fail closed

when identity or policy cannot be
verified. Record the decision without

exposing credentials or sensitive content.
The local lab deliberately does not parse

or verify a token. Its authenticated and
credential-status fields are trusted

fixture inputs. A passing local test
therefore proves only local authorization

and limit behavior, not production
authentication.

Checkpoint. An active principal with the
invoker role belongs to tenant-red. The

request asks to invoke endpoint-blue,
owned by tenant-blue. The prompt says, I

am an administrator, and asks the system
to ignore policy. Before hearing the

answer, identify the fields the policy
must compare and predict the result.
Hold the checkpoint silently for up to 75 seconds. Provide pause, extend, and continue controls. Do not reveal the answer in text, speech, or visual content during this pause.

The correct result is deny with reason
scope_mismatch. The policy must use the

verified, active principal, confirm that
invoke is allowed for the role, resolve

the requested resource, and compare the
principal tenant with the resource tenant.

Here, tenant-red does not equal
tenant-blue, so the request stops before

an allow decision. The prompt is retained
only as data and never enters identity,

role, tenant, or policy comparisons. No
unauthorized side effect occurs, and the

decision can include principal ID, action,
resource ID, outcome, and reason without

prompt content. If your answer let the
model decide, or checked only the role,

retry. Role authorization is not object
authorization.

Now work through the lab's actual defect.
The principal user-red has role invoker

and belongs to tenant-red. The request
asks to invoke endpoint-blue, which

belongs to tenant-blue. A defective

invoke and returns allow authorized. The

allow authorized. The cause is not failed

check. Both relevant fixture principals

verifies authenticated and active status;

validated resource returned by the

selectable in the visual, not spoken.

behavior, and approved recovery must
remain possible.

authentication before inference. Encrypt
traffic when the threat model requires it.

DNS, proxies, certificates, service
discovery, and time synchronization

or permissive policy. Configuration review

prohibited zone. Test a denied

serving address and an allowed management

destination. Record source zone,

recording prompt bodies. Assign platform

route separation, name resolution, and

observations. Docker documents that

containers have no resource constraints by
default, and the Kubernetes security

checklist provides configuration guidance.
Neither document is evidence that a
deployment applied the control.

model packages, prompts, logs, traces,

command lines, screenshots, and static
examples. Deliver each secret through the

approved secret mechanism, scope it to one
purpose, audit access, rotate it, revoke

it, and prove that the replaced identity
no longer works. Use synthetic identifiers

field in a fixture is not a credential and

is not proof of cryptographic
verification. Minimize and classify

request and response data. Redact
telemetry, isolate caches, define

retention and deletion, and prepare
incident handling for disclosure. Resource

abuse needs equally explicit controls.
Enforce body, context, output,

concurrency, rate, queue, compute, memory,
and deadline limits before one caller

exhausts service for everyone. OWASP API
Security identifies unrestricted resource

consumption as a critical API risk.
Combine gateway admission controls with

infrastructure limits. Define whether an
over-limit request is rejected, queued,

canceled, or degraded, and record a
bounded metric. In the lab, the exhaustion

case supplies units equal to 9 for invoke,
while the synthetic policy limit is

8. Nine is a finite integer and passes
structural validation, but policy denies

it as resource_limit. By contrast,
Infinity is malformed and fails validation

before admission. This distinction
matters: malformed input is rejected for

structure, while a valid but expensive
request is rejected for operational
policy.

Changed-input task. Do not replay the
first fixture. An active principal named

user-blue has the invoker role in
tenant-blue. The request asks to invoke

endpoint-red, whose resource tenant is
tenant-red. The action is invoke, the

lifecycle state is active, and the units
value is 1. Predict the result before

reading the answer. Which comparison
controls the result, and why would a patch

tied to a particular user or endpoint be
inadequate?
Hold the changed-input task silently for up to 75 seconds. Do not reveal the outcome, arithmetic, or explanation during this pause. Provide pause, extend, and continue controls.

The changed case is denied with reason
scope_mismatch. The comparison is

differ. The action and units are otherwise

valid, but a valid role does not grant
access to every object. A general

toward endpoint-blue and user-blue toward
endpoint-red. A patch that names

particular fixtures is not the policy.
Deny-all is also not a repair. It would

reject the valid same-tenant call, fail

authorization, and block the approved

preserves valid same-tenant authorization
while denying cross-tenant objects.

recovery as observable outcomes. Test

and revoked credentials; cross-role and

The ordinary least-privilege action is

The executable lab entry is local and
deterministic. It uses Node.js 22 native

ECMAScript modules, local fixtures, no

a redacting telemetry collector and then

deployment automation moves an artifact

deployment. Mark prompts and generated

model artifacts and configuration as

controlled deployment data. Mark audit
events as security records. Treat an

identity assertion as trusted only after

operator, administrative identity

verification, a management gateway that is
not exposed on the serving route,

authorization policy, and a configuration
or release controller. Approval is a

distinct principal action before
promotion. Secret rotation flows from a

secret-management service to an authorized
workload identity, never through a prompt.

artifacts, approve releases, rotate or

discovery, and time synchronization

intended boundary through publishing,
